name: Apigenin
lead: Apigenin (4',5,7-trihydroxyflavone) is a yellow plant flavone found in parsley, celery, celeriac and especially chamomile, where it makes up about 68 percent of the flavonoids in the flower heads.[1] It is sold as an over-the-counter supplement and is popular in sleep-stack discussion, usually alongside magnesium and theanine.

People who use it for their looks do so through recovery: the idea is that calmer evening wind-down and better sleep support skin condition, under-eye appearance, training recovery and body composition. This is a chain claimed by supplement users rather than a direct cosmetic effect.

In laboratory work apigenin binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, the basis of claims that it is calming, although studies disagree on how it interacts with that site.[1] Reviews describe a wide range of preclinical findings including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, neuroprotective and anticancer effects, along with limited solubility and absorption.[2][4][5]
Human work to date includes an absorption and metabolism study in healthy adults and several registered trials on other conditions.[6][7][8]

paras: Apigenin is mostly taken as a sleep and relaxation aid, and its appearance relevance is by way of sleep: communities that discuss it connect restful nights with clearer skin, less puffy eyes, and better gym recovery. It also appears in topical and skin-care discussions of plant flavonoids, where reviews of bee products and dermatology list flavones among skin-active ingredients.[9]

Dried parsley is the richest known food source, with fresh parsley and celery hearts supplying far less per serving, and chamomile tea is the best-known drink source.[1] Dietary-intake surveys and food-composition studies have measured apigenin alongside other flavonoids in vegetables and fruits.[10][11]

Apigenin is a yellow crystalline solid with low water solubility that has historically been used to dye wool.[1][3] It has a formula of C15H10O5 and exists in plants largely as glycosides such as apiin, vitexin and rhoifolin.[1] Plants make it from phenylalanine via the phenylpropanoid pathway, passing through naringenin, with flavone synthase enzymes forming the final product.[1]

In vitro work reports competitive binding to the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, and a 1995 study cited in encyclopedic summaries described anxiolytic-type activity.[1] A widely cited 1998 study also tested phytoestrogens, including apigenin, against estrogen receptor beta.[12] Grokipedia additionally describes inhibition of CD38 and elevation of NAD+, a description from an AI-generated source.[3]

In a study of healthy male adults, apigenin itself was poorly absorbed, with urinary metabolites equal to about 0.5 percent of intake over 24 hours; glucuronide and sulfate conjugates were the main metabolites, and the parsley glycoside form showed a distinct plasma profile.[6] A 2002 review of flavonoid bioavailability and safety likewise described limited absorption of the class.[13]

A 2019 review summarised preclinical work on apigenin across cancer, inflammation and neuroprotection and noted low solubility and bioavailability as obstacles.[2] A review of in vivo evidence covered animal and human data on diabetes, amnesia, depression and insomnia.[4] Laboratory studies have also examined apigenin with chemotherapy agents in colorectal cancer cells and its activity against viruses.[14][15]

No published trial of apigenin as a sleep or cosmetic aid was located. Registered human studies include a completed absorption, metabolism and excretion study in 17 healthy volunteers, published in 2022,[6][7] a trial of apigenin in elderly patients with sepsis,[8] and a supplement-combination study on stress and sleep (n=115) whose results have not been published.[16]

Other registered work includes a cardiovascular-risk trial in 100 participants,[17] a withdrawn trial in high-risk breast clinic patients,[18] a cryopreserved-sperm study with an apigenin medium,[19] and a chamomile and saffron trial in Parkinson disease.[20]

Apigenin has a place in online sleep-supplement routines, typically paired with magnesium and theanine. Forum users on strength sites also ask whether plant flavones affect hormones, a question linked to the estrogen-receptor research described above.[12]

timeline.event: Dutch dietary surveys begin quantifying flavonoid intake including apigenin.[10]
Study tests apigenin among phytoestrogens at estrogen receptor beta.[12]

lore.intro: Apigenin is discussed in sleep-stack conversation as the chamomile compound for falling asleep, and occasionally in hormone-focused threads.

claims.claim: Apigenin before bed improves sleep quality.
claims.believers: Users of sleep-supplement routines say it relaxes them via GABA activity and pair it with magnesium and theanine.
claims.experts: Laboratory studies show GABA-A binding but disagree on how it interacts, and no published trial results on apigenin and sleep were located; a sleep-and-stress supplement-combination study is registered.[1][16]

claims.claim: Apigenin inhibits CD38 and raises NAD+ for anti-aging.
claims.believers: Proponents cite the mechanism as the route to a more youthful, better-recovered body.
claims.experts: The claim is described in an AI-generated encyclopedia; preclinical reviews describe cell and animal work and low bioavailability.[2][3]

claims.believers: Some cautious users on training forums worry that plant flavones could affect hormones and masculine traits.
claims.experts: A 1998 study tested apigenin among phytoestrogens at estrogen receptor beta; a human absorption study found little unchanged apigenin reaches circulation.[12][6]

card.summary: Chamomile flavone in sleep stacks; GABA-binding in the lab, no sleep or looks trial found.
card.note: Estrogen-receptor activity has been studied in vitro.

quick.overview:
Apigenin is a flavone from chamomile, parsley and celery sold as a sleep supplement. It is popular in sleep stacks.

Lab studies show GABA receptor binding, but no controlled trial of sleep or appearance outcomes was found.
quick.mechanism: Binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors in vitro; other proposed mechanisms include CD38 inhibition.
quick.risks: Safety data in humans are limited; it has been tested at estrogen receptors in vitro. It is sold as a supplement.

chain: Chamomile-derived flavone sold as an evening supplement
Claimed calming effect and better sleep
Better recovery, skin and training consistency
angle.text: Users take apigenin in the evening as part of a sleep stack, hoping for better rest and recovery. Any visible payoff is therefore indirect: refreshed skin and eyes, and more consistent training.
